title: Syllabus
content:
Introduction to Second Language Acquisition (Postgraduate) # Note: This syllabus outlines the plan for a 12-week, seminar-style course. Minor adjustments may be made as we progress.
Course website: https://zjpsycholin.github.io/SLA4pg/ Instructor email: jzhang3@ahu.edu.cn
Course Description # This graduate seminar is a research-oriented introduction to how adults acquire second and additional languages. We emphasize linguistic architecture, cross-linguistic variation, interfaces, processing, and implications for teaching, using Slabakova (2016) as the anchor text. Part I establishes language architecture and variation; Part II situates L2 within broader acquisition contexts and highlights the role of input; Part III surveys adult L2 morphology, syntax, the mental lexicon, interfaces, processing, and classroom implications.
Learning Objectives # By the end of the course, students will be able to:
Explain major theoretical proposals in L2 acquisition and how they derive predictions. Critically evaluate empirical studies (design, measures, analyses, interpretations). Compare acquisition across modules (morphology, syntax, lexicon) and interfaces. Relate L2 processing findings (e.g., eye-tracking, ERP) to competence and instruction. Formulate testable research questions and design a feasible study. Articulate pedagogical implications (e.g., Bottleneck Hypothesis; focus on form). Methods of Instruction # Seminar discussions, mini-methods workshops, and hands-on data critique. Expect close reading, replication thinking, and constructive debate.
Instructional Materials # Required Text # Slabakova, R. (2016). Second Language Acquisition. Oxford University Press.
(Designed for advanced undergraduates/graduate students with prior linguistics knowledge; emphasizes generative SLA and empirical methods.) Recommended (background / triangulation) # Saville-Troike, M. (2015). Introducing Second Language Acquisition (3rd ed.). Cambridge University Press. Assessment & Grading # Participation & Attendance (10%) — consistent, informed contributions; Be prepared. Quizzes (20%, 5% * 4) — short quizzes on key concepts and theories. Quiz #1: Chapter 1 & 2 Quiz #2: Chapter 3 & 4 Quiz #3: Chapter 7 & 8 Quiz #4: Chapter 10 & 11 Questionsets(20%, 10% * 2) — questions on key concepts and theories. Questionset #1: chapters 1, 2, 3, & 4 Questionset #2: chapters 7, 8, 10, & 11 Final Research Proposal (50%) — 8–10 pages: motivation, literature, hypotheses, design, predicted outcomes. See “Term Research Proposal” for details. Total = 100%
12-Week Schedule (Topics • Chapters • Key Issues) # We read selectively and thematically; not every section of each chapter is assigned. Page-level reading lists will be posted weekly.
Note: We will not cover Ch. 6 or Ch. 13. Topics are calibrated for first-year MA students with no prior SLA background.
Week 1 — Language Architecture & SLA as a Science # Chapter: Slabakova Ch. 1
Topics: What counts as “knowledge of language”? Core modules (phonology, morphology, syntax, semantics, pragmatics); interfaces; what makes SLA scientific (theory → prediction → test).
Key issues: Evidence in SLA; competence vs. performance; why interfaces can be hard.
Week 2 — Cross-Linguistic Variation & the Learning Task # Chapter: Ch. 2
Topics: What varies across languages; features/parameters in plain language; why variation matters for L2 learning.
Key issues: Initial state and transfer (intuitive examples); falsifiable predictions without heavy formalisms.
Week 3 — Psychological Reality: Using Language in Real Time # Chapter: Ch. 3
Topics: What “processing” means; how the parser uses memory and cues; ambiguity resolution with simple examples.
Key issues: Distinguishing knowledge vs. processing; gentle intro to common tasks (e.g., acceptability judgments).
Week 4 — Age, Input & the Critical Period # Chapter: Ch. 4
Topics: Age effects (pronunciation vs. grammar/meaning); what “critical period” claims mean; role of input amount/quality.
Key issues: Measuring outcomes simply; clear expectations for different subsystems.
Week 5 — Acquisition of Functional Morphology # Chapter: Ch. 7
Topics: Inflectional morphology (tense, agreement) as a common bottleneck; classic findings explained simply (e.g., missing surface inflection, feature reassembly).
Key issues: Representation vs. performance explanations in plain terms; pedagogical implications.
Week 6 — Acquisition of Syntax (the Basics) # Chapter: Ch. 8
Topics: Word order basics; movement in everyday terms; how learners “reset” patterns from L1 to L2.
Key issues: What would count as evidence for/against full acquisition of a structure (no heavy formalism).
Week 7 & 8 — Syntax–Semantics Interface (Meaning that Depends on Structure) # Chapter: Ch. 10
Topics: Tense/aspect and other meaning contrasts that hinge on structure; common cross-linguistic mismatches students feel.
Key issues: Why interfaces can be tricky; simple diagnostics to notice interface delays.
Week 9 & 10 — Syntax–Discourse & Semantics–Pragmatics Interfaces # Chapter: Ch. 11
Topics: Topic/focus, pronouns, information structure; scalar implicatures and polite meaning beyond the literal.
Key issues: Mapping discourse/pragmatics to form in L2; approachable classroom tasks to probe these mappings.
Week 11 & 12 — L2 Processing & Gentle Methods Literacy # Chapter: Ch. 12
Topics: What common tasks look like (GJT, simple reading tasks); how to frame a tiny classroom diagnostic; basics of reliable evidence (controls, sample size at a glance).
Key issues: Linking competence claims to processing predictions—without statistics overload.
Weekly Workflow (Typical) # Before class: Read assigned chapters. In class: mini-lectures; student-led seminar; methods/data critique; discussion; synthesis. After class: Update proposal or methods task with new insights. Policies (Highlights) # Attendance & participation are essential to seminar learning. Academic integrity applies to all submissions (cite properly; no AI-generated text without disclosure and permission). Style: APA or LSA; be consistent.

title: Ch.1: Language architecture
content:
Chapter 1 — Language Architecture & SLA as a Science # Anchor text: Slabakova, R. (2016). Second Language Acquisition. Chapter 1: Language architecture. Link to Chapter 1
⭐ Overview # What it means to “know a language” and how that knowledge is organized into parts that work together. How SLA uses the scientific method (observe → generalize → hypothesize → test → revise) to make falsifiable predictions. Why theory-to-evidence links matter (e.g., richer agreement systems may correlate with null subjects) and how this connects to teaching relevance. 🎯 Learning goals # By the end of Week 1 you should be able to:
Describe, in your own words, what “knowledge of language” is. Name the main parts (sound, word pieces, structure, meaning, use) and say what each does. Explain the basic steps of SLA research (observe → hypothesize → test → revise) and why predictions matter. Give one simple learning/teaching implication that follows from these ideas. 📖 Reading (do before class) # Required: Slabakova (2016), Chapter 1 (focus on the big picture of §§1.1–1.4). Guiding questions while you read
What would count as evidence for/against a claim about L2 knowledge? Where in the architecture would you locate difficulties with agreement vs. word order? 🧠 Key terms # knowledge of language; competence vs. performance; lexicon; phonology; morphology; syntax; semantics; pragmatics; interface; hypothesis; prediction; falsifiability; transfer; null subject
🧩 Core content # 1) What does it mean to “know a language”? # We each carry an internal system that lets us understand and create new sentences. Competence = what you know; Performance = how it comes out in real life (with slips/hesitations). Try it: Think of a sentence you’ve never heard before but still understand—proof your mind can build new meanings from pieces. 2) The building blocks (“modules”) # Phonology: how a language uses sounds (mental categories/patterns). Morphology: meaningful pieces inside words (walk-ed, cat-s). Syntax: how words combine and move (word order, questions, negatives). Semantics: literal, compositional meaning. Pragmatics: meaning from context (implicature, politeness, what’s implied). Try it: Take any short sentence. Label what is sound-related, word-piece related, structure-related, literal meaning, and context-based. 3) Interfaces: when parts meet # Real communication requires coordination between parts (e.g., structure + meaning). Some cross-language differences live at these interfaces, which can feel tricky in an L2. Mini example: English red car vs. a language where the adjective follows the noun. Differences like this can ripple through usage and comprehension. 4) SLA as a science (gentle view) # Steps: observe → suggest an explanation → make a prediction → check whether the prediction holds → adjust if needed. Why “falsifiable”? Explanations should be clear enough that evidence could show them wrong if they’re wrong. Simple illustration (from Chapter 1 themes): If a learner’s L1 often leaves subjects unspoken (null subjects), we might predict more subject omission in their early L2 English—something we can check in beginner data. 5) Why this matters for learning/teaching # Different parts can be hard for different reasons (sound patterns vs. small endings vs. word order vs. meaning-in-context). Knowing the parts helps you notice patterns, set goals, and choose strategies (e.g., targeted listening for sound contrasts; focused reading for small endings; chunking for word order). Activity 1: Error Detective: Grammar Investigation Practice # 🔍 Your Mission # Work with a partner to find and fix common English errors. Think like a detective - spot what’s wrong, correct it, and explain why it needs fixing!
🕵️‍♂️ Investigation Time # Part 1: Spot the Errors # Read these 16 sentences. Put a checkmark (✓) next to any that sound unnatural or incorrect.
Ø Rains a lot here. [L1: Spanish] Car red is new. [L1: French] Yesterday he go to school. [L1: Mandarin] Cat is on table. [L1: Russian] She eat breakfast every day. [L1: Arabic] Always he is late. [L1: Turkish] Teacher give book to student yesterday. [L1: Mandarin] People is friendly here. [L1: Portuguese] It raining now. [L1: Korean] I bought three book. [L1: Thai] Very the movie I liked. [L1: German] He not understands. [L1: Italian] On the table is a cup my. [L1: Japanese] She is in the home. [L1: Arabic] I saw big very dog. [L1: Korean] Yesterday was cold, Ø didn’t wear jacket. [L1: Spanish] Part 2: Fix the Errors # For each one:
Underline the problem area Rewrite the sentence correctly Explain the fix in simple terms Example:
Original: Rains a lot here. Fixed: It rains a lot here. Explanation: Needs subject “it” for weather Helpful Explanation Labels: # Missing subject (need it) Wrong word order Wrong tense (past/present) Missing a/the Missing -s ending Wrong verb form Missing helper verb (do/does) Possessive error Wrong preposition Part 3: Explain what causes these errors. # 🎯 Quick Practice # Let’s try two examples together:
Sentence 3: Yesterday he go to school.
Problem: _________________ Fix: _____________________ Reason: __________________ Sentence 10: I bought three book.
Problem: _________________ Fix: _____________________ Reason: __________________ 💡 Helpful Notes # Common Error Patterns: # Spanish speakers: Often miss subject pronouns (“Rains” → “It rains”) French speakers: May put adjectives after nouns (“car red” → “red car”) Mandarin speakers: Might forget past tense (“go” → “went”) and articles (“the teacher”) Arabic speakers: May forget the -s ending (“eat” → “eats”) Korean speakers: Might struggle with word order (“big very” → “very big”) Discussion Questions: # Which errors were easiest to spot? Why? Which were hardest to correct? Why? Did you notice any patterns in the errors? How might knowing a student’s first language help you teach English? Activity 2 — Mini H→P→T Lab (Hypothesis → Prediction → Test) # 🎯 Your Mission # Become a language researcher for a day! Design a tiny experiment to test how people learn English grammar patterns. You’ll follow the same scientific process that real researchers use.
Starter prompts
Null-subject correlation: If L1 licenses null subjects but L2 does not, early L2 English shows subject omission in production/acceptability. Aspect packaging difference: If L1 distributes aspect with particles/auxiliaries but L2 ties aspect to verb morphology, beginners under-mark or mis-map aspect in narratives. Procedure # Hypothesis — 1–2 sentences tied to architecture (point out module/interface & features). Prediction — Specify group (L1), behavior (what measure), and locus (where in structure). Micro-test — Pick one task: Tiny Grammaticality Judgement Task (8–10 items; 4 critical + 4 controls; binary/4-point scale), or Picture-elicited production (4 pictures; target one structure), or Mini reading (4 sentences with 1 Q each targeting the property).
Define metric (e.g., % omissions; % “acceptable”; % correct choice) and a falsifier. Peer critique — Swap designs; check confounds (length, vocabulary, context, uncontrolled L1 mix). Wrap — present; you trace each step to Observe → Hypothesize → Test → Revise. 🎓 Examples for Inspiration # Example Study 1: The “It” Problem # Hypothesis: Spanish speakers omit “it” in weather sentences Prediction: 60% omission rate in fill-in-blank tasks Test: 8 sentence completion items Metric: % of missing “it” in required contexts Falsifier: If omission rate < 20% Example Study 2: The “-ed” Problem # Hypothesis: Mandarin speakers forget past tense endings Prediction: 50% error rate in picture description Test: 4 past event pictures Metric: Number of missing “-ed” endings Falsifier: If error rate < 10% ✅ Tasks # Before class (preview) # Read Chapter 1 for the big picture; don’t worry about technical detail. Skim “Teaching relevance” notes. Jot down one L2 feature that puzzles you (e.g., articles, agreement, word order, polite meaning). During class (light activities) # Spot-the-part: Label 3–4 sentences for sound, word pieces, structure, literal meaning, and context. Prediction postcard: Write: “If X is true in L1, then beginners might Y in L2.” Keep it concrete and short (one sentence). Practice (micro-lab you can try) # Prompt (approachable): “If L1 allows null subjects but L2 does not, beginners may omit subjects in early L2 English.”
Prediction: beginners from a null-subject L1 omit subjects more often than those from a non-null-subject L1. Simple check: look at a handful of beginner sentences (text or short speech) and note presence/absence of subjects. What would falsify it? No difference across L1 groups, or consistent subjects even at the start. After class (review) # Short reflection:
One idea from Ch. 1, in your own words. One prediction it suggests for L2 learners. One easy way to check that prediction (e.g., a tiny noticing task in readings this week). Self-check:
(1) Define falsifiability and explain why it matters in SLA.
(2) Give one predicted correlation between morphology and syntax.
(3) Why are “Teaching relevance” boxes included?
(4) List the steps of the scientific method in SLA.
(5) Where in the architecture would you locate difficulty with verb movement vs. agreement endings?
🧭 Preview of Week 2 # Next we look at language variation (how languages differ) and why that shapes the SLA learning task—including which features may transfer from L1 and which need new learning.

title: Ch.2: Language Variation
content:
Chapter 2 — Language Variation & the Learning Task" # Anchor text: Slabakova, R. (2016). Second Language Acquisition. Chapter 2: Language variation.
Link to Chapter 2
⭐ Overview # How languages differ and what that means for learning a second language. Where variation “lives” in the grammar today (hint: features in the functional lexicon) and why that matters for learners. How prior knowledge from the L1 transfers into the L2 starting point, and what “resetting” involves. Why some areas (e.g., functional morphology and mismatched feature cues) tend to be harder. 🎯 Learning goals # By the end of Week 2 you should be able to:
Explain (in plain language) where many cross-language differences come from. Describe the idea of L1 transfer as the initial state and what it predicts. Give one concrete example of how a feature mapping/mismatch can make learning harder. Sketch a simple “if…then” prediction for learner behavior based on a parametric difference. 📖 Reading (do before class) # Required: Slabakova (2016), Chapter 2 (focus on §§2.1–2.4 big picture). As you skim: note any places where the book connects variation → specific learning tasks. Guiding questions while you read
Where does the chapter locate most variation today (lexicon? interfaces?) and why? If your L1 and L2 differ on some feature (e.g., subject expression, word order), what prediction would that make for early L2? 🧠 Key terms # principles & parameters; Minimalist Program; functional lexicon; grammatical features; PF/LF interfaces; transfer; parameter “resetting”; feature exponents; clustering; compounding parameter; learning task
CHAPTER 2: LANGUAGE VARIATION # Preview Focus: This chapter explains why languages differ systematically and how these differences affect second language learning. By the end, you’ll understand:
How languages vary in structure (and why these variations aren’t random) Key theoretical frameworks for explaining variation Why some aspects of second language acquisition are harder than others 2.1 How Do Languages Differ? # Languages vary in three main ways, but syntactic (sentence structure) differences are the most systematic:
1. Surface-Level Differences # Lexicon: Different words for the same thing (e.g., English “table” = Bulgarian “masa”). These must be learned individually. Phonotactics: Rules for combining sounds (e.g., English forbids words starting with “tl-”, but Bulgarian allows it: tlăst = “fat”). 2. Syntactic Variation: Word Order Patterns # Syntactic differences follow harmony—languages are consistent in how they arrange “heads” (key words) and their “complements” (supporting information):
Head-initial: Head comes before complement (e.g., English: “to the store” [Preposition + NP]; “eat food” [Verb + NP]). Head-final: Head comes after complement (e.g., Japanese: “kōen ni” [NP + Postposition]; “ringo o taberu” [NP + Verb]). Major Word Order Types (from 1377 languages studied):
41% SOV (e.g., Japanese: Taro Hanako-ni hon-o ageta = “Taro gave Hanako a book”) 35.4% SVO (e.g., English: “Taro gave Hanako a book”) 7% VSO (e.g., Irish: “Chonaic mé an cat” = “Saw I the cat”) 3. Exceptional Cases: Polysynthetic Languages # Languages like Mohawk use:
Free word order: Meaning doesn’t depend on word position Noun incorporation: Nouns are built into verbs (e.g., wa-sh-ako-hsir-u = “he-her-blanket-gave”) Morphology for meaning: Verb endings signal “who did what to whom” (not word order). 2.2 Principles and Parameters (P&P) Theory # This framework explains why languages vary systematically:
Key Concepts # Principles: Universal rules shared by all languages (e.g., Every sentence must have a subject). Parameters: “Switches” that create differences between languages. Setting one parameter explains multiple related features. Examples of Parameters # Head Directionality Parameter: Explains head-initial (English) vs. head-final (Japanese) structures. Null Subject Parameter (NSP): On (e.g., Spanish/Italian): Allows missing subjects (Habla español = “He speaks Spanish”) and has rich verb agreement. Off (e.g., English): Requires explicit subjects (“He speaks Spanish”) and has limited verb agreement. Compounding Parameter: Determines if a language allows noun-noun compounds (spider box in English) and verb-particle phrases (eat up). 2.3 The Minimalist Program # A newer framework that simplifies P&P:
Universal Syntax: All languages use the same basic operation (Merge) to build sentences. Sources of Variation: Differences come from: Functional morphology: Tense/agreement markers (e.g., Spanish -a vs. English -s for 3rd person singular). Phonetic Form (PF): Which part of a moved phrase is pronounced (e.g., English moves “what” in questions; Mandarin leaves it in place). Logical Form (LF): How meaning depends on context (e.g., Mandarin uses context, not articles, to signal definiteness). 2.4 What Do Second Language Learners Need to Learn? # Initial State: Learners start with their first language (L1) grammar and transfer its rules/parameters to the second language (L2). Challenges: Resetting parameters when L1 and L2 differ (e.g., a Spanish speaker learning English must learn to use explicit subjects). Mastering functional morphology (tense, agreement, articles)—this is the “bottleneck” of acquisition. Predictions: Easy: Features shared by L1 and L2 (e.g., SVO word order for English learners of French). Hard: Feature mismatches (e.g., English past tense vs. Spanish imperfect) and context-dependent meaning (e.g., Mandarin definiteness). Key Terms to Know # Head vs. Complement: Key word vs. supporting information in a phrase Harmony: Consistency in head-complement order across phrases Parameter: A “switch” explaining cross-linguistic differences Functional morphology: Grammatical markers (tense, agreement) Bottleneck Hypothesis: Functional morphology is the hardest part of L2 acquisition Preview Questions # How does the Head Directionality Parameter explain differences between English and Japanese? Why do Spanish learners of English often omit subjects (e.g., Speaks Spanish)? What makes functional morphology harder to learn than word order? ✅ Tasks # Before class (preview) # Read Ch. 2 for the main ideas (don’t get lost in technical terms). Bring one L1 ↔ L2 difference you’ve noticed (word order? subject expression? compounding?). We’ll use it to make a prediction. In class # Feature hunt: Pick one L1↔L2 contrast and say which feature(s) might be different and how they surface. “If-then” hypothesis: Write one sentence: “If L1 has X, then beginners may Y in L2.” Keep it observable (Y should be something you can count or notice). Practice # Prompt (approachable): “If a learner’s L1 freely drops subjects but the L2 does not, early L2 subject omission should be higher for that learner group.”
Design idea: Compare a few beginner sentences (two L1 groups). Count subject present/absent. What would falsify it? No group difference; or consistent subjects from the start.
(This mirrors how Chapter 2 turns theory into learning tasks and predictions.) After class (review) # Mini reflection (≈150–200 words):
Name one L1↔L2 difference in features or feature exponents. Write an if-then prediction it suggests. One easy way you could check it (e.g., quick corpus search; classroom samples). Self-check (answers hidden):
(1) Where does the Minimalist view largely locate variation?
(2) Why can feature–form mismatches be hard for L2 learners?
(3) What does L1 transfer predict about the initial L2 grammar?
(4) State one area often predicted to be harder than narrow syntax.
🧭 Preview of Week 3 # We shift from what varies to how language is processed: what the parser does online and how processing interacts with grammatical knowledge.

title: Ch.3: The Psychological Reality of Language in Use
content:
Chapter 3 — The Psychological Reality of Language in Use # Anchor text: Slabakova, R. (2016). Second Language Acquisition. Chapter 3: The psychological reality of language in use. Link to Chapter 3
⭐ Overview # What “processing” means: how the mind builds meaning in real time during listening/reading and plans forms during speaking. Big ideas: the parser, timing, limited resources, and why learners sometimes rely on easier cues (semantics/discourse) over costly structure when time is tight. What common methods actually measure (self-paced reading, eye-tracking, ERP) and how to read their basic signals. Why this matters: classroom input and tasks can shape processing (e.g., highlighting small forms, pacing, repeated exposure). 🎯 Learning goals # By the end of Week 3 you should be able to:
Explain, in plain terms, what the parser does and why time/attention matter. Recognize what self-paced reading, eye-tracking, and ERPs can tell us about L2 processing. State one simple prediction about when L2 learners might rely more on meaning cues than syntax (and why). Suggest one teaching move that eases processing demands for a difficult form. 📖 Reading (do before class) # Required: Slabakova (2016), Chapter 3 (read for big picture; you don’t need technical detail). As you skim, note: which findings suggest time pressure or memory limits shape L2 behavior? Guiding questions while you read
What’s the difference between “having a rule” and using it quickly while reading/listening? Which cues (lexical meaning, word order, agreement endings, discourse context) feel fast/easy vs. slow/costly? 🧠 Key terms # parser; incremental processing; garden-path; Good-Enough comprehension; cue-based retrieval; working memory; surprisal/predictability; self-paced reading (SPR); eye-tracking; regressions; ERP (N400, P600); ambiguity resolution; speed–accuracy trade-off
Lecture notes # Core Goal: Understand how the brain processes language (speech/reading) and links linguistic structure to psychology—critical for language learning.
3.1 Sentence Comprehension: Basic Process # A fast, 5-step sequence (not just “hearing words”):
Store incoming sounds in short-term memory. Split continuous speech into words (no “gaps” in speech). Retrieve word meaning/grammar from the mental lexicon (internal “dictionary”). Build grammatical structure (parsing) to organize words. Use context/world knowledge to clarify meaning. Note: Speech is language’s primary medium (children learn it first; most languages lack writing).
3.2 Phonological Perception & Lexical Recognition # 1. Speech Challenges # No word boundaries: Unlike writing, speech has no pauses between words (see textbook Figure 3.1). Coarticulation: Sounds blend (e.g., French avec vous → /aveg vu/; k becomes g before voiced v). 2. Pre-Lexical Cues (Segmenting Speech) # Rhythm (stressed/unstressed syllables) and tone (Mandarin/Thai) help split the sound stream. 3. Lexical Recognition Models # Adult English speakers store 50,000–100,000 words; recognition is competitive:
Model How It Works Example: Recognizing “February” Cohort Model 1. Activate words matching first 1–2 sounds (“cohort”). 2. Filter mismatches as more sounds arrive. 1. /fe/ → fence, phenomenon, February 2. /b/ → only February remains TRACE Model Words activate on a scale (more match = higher activation); no strict cohort. /fe/ boosts fence; /b/ shifts activation to February Consensus: Multiple words activate in parallel; competition narrows to the best match.
3.3 Morphology: Whole Words or Morphemes? # Morphemes = smallest meaningful units (e.g., book-s = book [lexical] + -s [plural, functional]).
1. Key Morphology Types # Type Role Example Lexical Morphemes Core meaning (free) walk, happy Functional Morphemes Grammatical meaning (bound/free) -ed, the Inflectional Add grammar (no category change) walk-ed (still verb) Derivational Change meaning/category happy-ness (Adj→N) 2. Great Past Tense Debate # Words & Rules: Irregulars (ate) = whole words; Regulars (walked) = built by rule (verb + -ed). Connectionist: Both = whole words; activation depends on use frequency. Consensus: High-frequency words (happiness) = whole units; low-frequency (disenchantment) = decomposed. 3.4 The Syntactic Parser # Builds grammatical structure (phrase trees) to understand “who did what.”
1. Structure = Interpretation # Example: Mary ate the cake in the dining room
Interpretation 1: Cake was in the dining room (NP-attachment: the cake [in the dining room]). Interpretation 2: Eating was in the dining room (VP-attachment: ate [the cake in the dining room]). 2. Garden Path Sentences # Temporary ambiguity tricks the parser (needs reanalysis):
Example: The tomcat curled up on the cushion seemed friendly 1st wrong analysis: The tomcat curled up… (complete sentence). Trigger: seemed (reveals curled up = reduced relative clause). 3.5 Models of Syntactic Processing # Debate: When do we use syntax vs. semantics/context?
Model Type Core Idea Example: The defendant/evidence examined by the lawyer… Modular (Garden Path) 2-stage: Syntax first, then semantics. Heuristics: Late Closure/Minimal Attachment. No difference between defendant (animate) and evidence (inanimate). Interactive (Constraint-Based) 1-stage: Use all info (syntax/semantics) at once. Parallel structure activation. Defendant (animate = likely Agent) is harder; evidence (inanimate) is easier. Dependency Locality Theory Focuses on complexity: Storage (hold words) + Integration (connect distant words) costs. Object relatives (The reporter who the senator attacked) are harder than subject relatives. 3.6 Working Memory # Active workspace for language (short-term, different from long-term memory).
Measure Task Tests Phonological Short-Term Memorize digits/words. Pure storage Reading Span Read sentences + remember last words. Storage + processing Debate Outcome: More support for dedicated resources—parsing (automatic) uses separate memory from conscious tasks.
3.7 Why This Matters # Grammar = “resting engine”; Parsing = “engine running” (Juffs & Rodriguez 2015)—they’re the same system. Processing shapes theory: Multiple Spell-Out (split sentences into chunks) reduces memory load. Learner difficulty: Complex structures (e.g., object relatives) tax processing, not just grammar knowledge. Key Terms # Mental Lexicon: Internal word storage. Coarticulation: Sound blending across words. Syntactic Parser: Builds grammatical structure. Garden Path Sentence: Temporarily ambiguous. Working Memory: Active language processing storage. Preview/Review Questions # Preview # Why is speech harder to segment than writing? What is a “garden path sentence”? Review # How do Cohort and TRACE models differ? Why are object relative clauses harder to process? What’s the evidence for dedicated working memory resources? ✅ Tasks # Before class (preview) # Read Chapter 3 for the big picture (don’t worry about technical terms). Jot down one sentence that misled you at first read (a mini garden-path or tricky agreement). In class (light activities) # Garden-path live: Three short ambiguous sentences; mark where your interpretation flips. Share which cue (syntax/meaning/punctuation) fixed it. Signal decoder: Given a simple plot (fake data) of SPR or eye-tracking, say where the difficulty happened and why (one sentence). Practice (micro-lab you can try) # Prompt: “When time is tight, learners rely more on meaning/plausibility than fine structure.”
Design idea: Create 6 short items where syntax conflicts with a plausible reading (e.g., agreement or filler–gap). Check: In a quick yes/no acceptability or timed choice, do learners prefer the plausible option over the strictly grammatical one? Falsifier: No plausibility bias (or a stronger structure bias) even under time pressure. After class (review) # Mini reflection (≈150–200 words):
Describe a case where you caught yourself using Good-Enough comprehension. Say which cue you favored (meaning? word order? morphology?) and why. One idea to train the less-used cue next week. Self-check (answers hidden):
(1) Why do garden-path sentences cause slowdowns?
(2) Define similarity-based interference in cue-based retrieval.
(3) Give one reason online measures can diverge from offline accuracy in L2.
(4) What pattern would support a processing (not competence) account for an L2 difficulty?
(5) Name one ERP component associated with morpho-syntactic violations and its interpretation.
📖 Additional resources (short articles/chapters) # Clahsen, H., & Felser, C. (2006). Grammatical processing in language learners. Applied Psycholinguistics, 27(1), 3–42. Kaan, E. (2014). Predictive sentence processing in L2 and L1. Linguistic Approaches to Bilingualism, 4(2), 257–282. Cunnings, I. (2017). Interference in native and non-native sentence processing. Bilingualism: Language and Cognition, 20(4), 712–721. Hopp, H. (2010). Ultimate attainment in L2 inflection: Moving beyond age. Second Language Research, 26(1), 129–160. Jegerski, J. (2016). Self-paced reading in SLA research. In The Routledge Handbook of SLA (methods chapter; short and practical). 🧭 Preview of Week 4 # Next we look at age, input, and the critical period debate—how outcomes differ across subsystems (pronunciation vs. morphosyntax/meaning) and how input quality/quantity fits into the picture.

title: Ch.4: The Critical Period Hypothesis (CPH)
content:
Chapter 4 — The Critical Period Hypothesis (CPH) # Anchor text: Slabakova, R. (2016). Second Language Acquisition. Chapter 4: The Critical Period Hypothesis. Link to Chapter 4
⭐ Overview # What the Critical Period Hypothesis (CPH) claims and why age might matter for language learning. How age of acquisition (AoA) interacts with input amount/quality, use, and education. Why age effects differ across subsystems: phonology (accent) vs. morphosyntax/semantics (mixed evidence). What counts as persuasive evidence (tasks, outcomes, controls) and what would falsify a strong CPH claim. 🎯 Learning goals # By the end of Week 4 you should be able to:
Explain the basic idea of a critical/sensitive period for L2 and the kinds of evidence used to test it. Distinguish AoA from other predictors (length of residence, input quality, education, use). Describe why phonology typically shows stronger age effects than morphosyntax/semantics. Write one if–then prediction about age and outcomes, and say what result would challenge that prediction. 📖 Reading (do before class) # Required: Slabakova (2016), Chapter 4 (read for big picture). As you read, note: Which results support a sharp cut-off vs. a gradual (sensitive) period? What confounds did studies try to control? Guiding questions while you read
Is there one “critical” period or are there multiple timelines for different subsystems? What would falsify a strong CPH (e.g., late starters reaching native-like levels under strict controls)? 🧠 Key terms # critical period; sensitive period; AoA (age of acquisition); length of residence (LoR); input amount/quality; ultimate attainment; near-native; confound; phonology vs. morphosyntax; aptitude; practice/use; outcome measures
Key Chapter Goal # Answer: Does biology limit when we can acquire a first (L1) or second (L2) language natively?
4.1 The View from Biology # Core Idea # Critical periods (biological “windows” for learning) are not unique to humans—they support the CPH for language.
Key Examples # Cross-Species Precedents
Songbirds: Zebra finches learn normal songs only if exposed to adult songs by 50 days old; canaries relearn annually (Nottebohm 1984). Cats: Kittens deprived of visual input before 8 weeks have permanent blindness (Hubel & Wiesel 1963)—parallels human brain plasticity decline. Human Neural Development
Plasticity: Children recover language after left hemisphere damage; adults do not (Lenneberg 1967). Lateralization: Language localizes to left hemisphere (Broca’s/Wernicke’s areas) by puberty—CPH ends when lateralization completes. Lenneberg’s (1967) CPH Evidence
Feral child Genie (discovered at 13, no language input): Never mastered complex syntax. 4.2 The Two Positions in L2 Acquisition # Debate: Does CPH Apply to L2? # Position 1: CPH Applies to L2 Position 2: CPH Does Not Apply to L2 Claim: L2 nativelikeness declines sharply after puberty. Claim: Age effects are gradual (no puberty cutoff) and input-driven. Example: Johnson & Newport (1989): 46 Chinese/Korean L2 English learners—AoA <15 = linear score decline; AoA >15 = flat scores. Example: Bialystok & Hakuta (1994): 2,000+ immigrants—late learners (AoA >20) with high education/residence scored near-native. 4.3 Modular Sensitive Periods (Not Global Nativelikeness) # Core Idea # No single “CPH for L2”—different grammar components have distinct biological windows.
Grammar Component Sensitive Period End Key Example Phonology (accent) ~6–8 years Birdsong 2005: L2 Spanish learners (AoA >12) = non-native vowels. Morphology (tense/agreement) ~10–12 years DeKeyser 2000: L2 French learners (AoA >10) struggled with past tense -é. Syntax (phrase structure) ~15–18 years White 2003: L2 English learners (AoA >20) mastered wh-movement. Semantics (meaning) Nearly open Kroll & Stewart 1994: No age effect on L2 semantic priming. Example: Hyltenstam & Abrahamsson (2003) # L2 Swedish learners (AoA 11–22): Near-native syntax but non-native accent—proves modularity.
4.4 L1-L2 as “Communicating Vessels” # Core Idea # L1 and L2 share cognitive resources—knowledge transfers between them (L1→L2 or L2→L1).
Key Examples # L1→L2 Transfer: Flege (1995): L1 English/L2 Spanish learners (AoA >12) transferred English /r/ (retroflex) to Spanish /r/ (trill). L2→L1 Attrition: Kupisch & Rothman (2011): L1 German child bilinguals (L2 English-dominant) made L1 gender errors. 4.5 Bilinguals: Not “Two Monolinguals in One Mind” # Core Idea # Bilinguals have integrated grammars (shared representations for overlapping features).
Evidence Against “Two Monolinguals” # Code-Switching: Poplack (1980): Spanish-English bilinguals only switch at shared syntactic boundaries (e.g., Yo saw the movie = okay; *I vi la película = not okay). Cross-Linguistic Priming: Kroll & Stewart (1994): L1 casa (Spanish) speeded L2 house (English) recognition. 4.6 & 4.7 The Importance of Input # Core Idea # Sensitive periods = “opportunity windows”; input = “fuel”—no input = no acquisition.
Key Examples # Input Necessity: Victor of Aveyron (feral child, no input) = no complex language. Input Quality: Long (1996): L2 learners with interactive input (feedback) mastered past tense -ed 2x faster than passive input. Indirect Evidence: Fossilization: Adult L2 English learners (no feedback) = persistent 3SG -s errors (*He walk). Creoles: Hawaiian Creole English (HCE): Children turned simplified pidgin input into a full grammar (e.g., tense marking: He bin work = past). Chapter 4 Takeaways # Biology (sensitive periods) sets limits, but input determines if those limits matter. L2 acquisition: Phonology/morphology are most age-vulnerable; syntax/semantics are more accessible late. Bilinguals have integrated grammars—L1 and L2 interact dynamically. ✅ Tasks # Before class (preview) # Read Ch. 4 for the big picture (don’t stress about statistics). Note one result you found persuasive and one you found questionable, and why. In class (light activities) # Curve sketching (pairs, 8–10 min): Draw three possible AoA→attainment curves (step, linear decline, steep-then-flat). Label which subsystem each curve might reflect. Confound detective (small groups, 10 min): Given a short study description, list at least three confounds to control (e.g., LoR, input quality, literacy). Practice (micro-lab you can try) # Prompt: “AoA predicts accent strength more strongly than morphosyntax outcomes.”
Plan: Collect (or imagine) small samples for accent ratings and a morphosyntax judgment score, each paired with AoA. Prediction: AoA correlates more tightly with accent than with morphosyntax. Falsifier: Comparable (or stronger) AoA correlation for morphosyntax after controlling LoR and input. After class (review) # Mini reflection (≈150–200 words): State one if–then prediction about AoA and an outcome you care about. Name two confounds you would control and one way to measure success. Self-check (answers hidden): What’s the difference between critical and sensitive period claims?
Why is phonology often more age-sensitive than morphosyntax?
Give two confounds that can mimic age effects.
What would falsify a hard CPH?
State one falsifiable prediction of a strong CPH for L2.
Give an example where measure choice changes the age conclusion.
Define input quality and give a diagnostic example.
Name two covariates that must be controlled in AoA studies.
What result would favor a sensitive-period over a strict CPH?
📖 Additional resources (short articles/chapters) # Johnson, J. S., & Newport, E. L. (1989). Critical period effects in second language learning. Cognitive Psychology, 21(1), 60–99. Birdsong, D., & Molis, M. (2001). On the evidence for maturational constraints in SLA. Journal of Memory and Language, 44(2), 235–249. DeKeyser, R. M. (2000). The robustness of critical period effects in second language acquisition. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, 22(4), 499–533. Flege, J. E., Yeni-Komshian, G., & Liu, S. (1999). Age constraints on second-language acquisition. Journal of Memory and Language, 41(1), 78–104. Long, M. H. (1990). Maturational constraints on language development. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, 12(3), 251–285. 🧭 Preview of Week 5 # Next we compare acquisition contexts: two first languages (2L1), child L2, multilingual and heritage learners—and what these profiles teach us about mechanisms of L2 development.
–>

title: Questionset1
content:
After-Class Research Task: Analyzing Real Second Language Morphosyntactic Data # A Mini Research Project on Interlanguage Morphosyntax** # Deadline: April 17th, 2026 # Task Overview # In this task, you will carry out a small-scale second language acquisition (SLA) research project based on real learner data. Your goal is to collect, organize, and analyze authentic second language data in order to identify morphosyntactic patterns, formulate generalizations, and develop theoretically informed hypotheses about learner knowledge and interlanguage development.
This task requires a more explicit connection between data analysis, SLA theory, and research methodology.
Learning Objectives # By completing this task, you should be able to:
collect and document authentic second language learner data in an ethical and systematic way identify and classify morphosyntactic patterns in learner production develop data-based generalizations about learner morphosyntactic knowledge formulate theoretically informed hypotheses about learner grammar and development connect empirical observations to concepts and debates in SLA research present a concise academic-style mini analysis Analytical Focus: Morphosyntax # Your analysis must focus on second language morphosyntactic knowledge.
Possible morphosyntactic domains # tense and aspect subject–verb agreement finiteness articles and definiteness plural morphology auxiliary systems negation interrogative formation pronouns and case copula and existential constructions word order subordination infinitives and gerunds relative clauses argument structure patterns nominal agreement functional morphology more broadly Advice on feature selection # Choose a feature set that:
appears multiple times in your dataset allows you to observe variation or stability can support pattern-based analysis rather than sentence-by-sentence commentary can be meaningfully linked to SLA theory Part 1. Collect Real Learner Data # Your task # Collect a small but analyzable dataset of real second language production.
The learner(s) may be:
international students classmates or colleagues who are L2 users friends or family members learning a second language any accessible learner of English or another target language Minimum data requirements # You must collect one of the following:
at least 50 learner-produced sentences
Factors to consider
proficiency levels first language backgrounds learning contexts lengths of exposure to the target language Data source requirements # The data must be:
produced by the learner(s), not copied from textbooks, websites, apps, or AI tools either spoken, written, or a combination of both rich enough for morphosyntactic analysis collected in a way that preserves the original learner forms Part 2. Recommended Data Collection Methods # Option A. Semi-structured interview # Conduct a short interview designed to elicit natural production across different time frames and structures.
Suggested prompts:
Can you describe your daily routine? What did you do last weekend? Tell me about your language learning experience. What are your plans for the future? Describe a difficult or memorable experience. What do you think makes a good teacher or student? Have you ever learned another language before? Option B. Picture-based elicitation # Use one picture or a sequence of pictures to elicit narrative or descriptive language.
You may target structures such as:
tense and aspect clause linking reference tracking word order agreement nominal morphology Option C. Guided writing # Ask the learner to produce a short written text of about 200–400 words on one of the following:
My experience learning English A challenge I faced recently Differences between studying in two places My future goals A memorable event My opinion about language learning Option D. Targeted elicitation # Design a focused task to elicit a particular morphosyntactic domain, for example:
tense/aspect contrasts article use plural marking question formation negation relative clauses agreement patterns If you choose this option, explain clearly why your elicitation design is appropriate for the feature you want to study.
Part 3. Ethical Guidelines # Before collecting the data:
explain that the data will be used for a course assignment obtain the learner’s permission do not include the learner’s real name in the submission anonymize all identifying information Use a pseudonym such as:
Learner A Participant 1 Speaker X If you audio-record spoken data, make sure the learner agrees to being recorded.
Part 4. Data Preparation and Transcription # Present the learner data in a clear and consistent format.
Formatting rules # number each sentence or utterance preserve the learner’s original wording do not silently correct non-target-like forms if needed, add the intended meaning in parentheses for spoken data, you may lightly clean false starts or fillers, but do not remove relevant grammatical evidence if you omit part of a longer utterance, use [...] Example # He go to school every day. Yesterday I am very tired because I finish assignment late. She doesn’t likes coffee. I have seen him last week. There is many students in the classroom. Part 5. Required Analytical Steps # Step 1. Describe the dataset # Briefly describe:
who the learner is in general terms the learner’s L1 background if relevant the target language the collection method the amount and type of data any relevant contextual factors such as length of study or learning environment Step 2. Identify recurring patterns # Look for repeated morphosyntactic behaviors.
Ask questions such as:
Which forms are used accurately and consistently? Which forms are variable? Which forms are omitted, overgeneralized, or used in non-target-like ways? Do the same patterns recur across contexts? Is there evidence of partial rule knowledge? Step 3. Group and code the data # Organize the examples into categories.
Possible categories include:
target-like use omission overgeneralization substitution non-target word order variability across similar contexts You may present your dataset in a small coding table if useful.
Step 4. Generalize from the data # Write 3–5 generalizations about the learner’s interlanguage grammar.
Your generalizations should be pattern-based, not anecdotal.
Step 5. Develop hypotheses # Propose 2–4 theoretically informed hypotheses.
Your hypotheses may draw on concepts such as:
interlanguage development transfer from the first language developmental constraints underspecification of functional morphology limited morphological realization despite syntactic knowledge input frequency and salience variability and processing pressure form–function mismatch feature reassembly interface-related difficulty Step 6. Connect to SLA literature # Briefly relate your findings to at least 2 academic sources from SLA literature.
You may use the literature to:
support an interpretation compare your learner with known developmental tendencies highlight a debate explain why the pattern matters theoretically You do not need a full literature review, but you should show that your analysis is informed by SLA research.
Part 6. Suggested Guiding Questions # You may use the following questions to guide your analysis:
What does the learner appear to know about the target structure? What remains unstable or inconsistent? Are the non-target-like forms random, or do they reflect a pattern? Is there evidence of systematic variability? Could the pattern reflect transfer, developmental sequence, processing limitations, or input effects? Does the learner show stronger control of lexical meaning than grammatical morphology? What does this dataset suggest about the learner’s current interlanguage system? Part 7. Suggested Report Structure # 1. Introduction # Briefly state the purpose of the task and identify the morphosyntactic feature(s) you will analyze.
2. Learner Background and Data Collection # Provide a short description of the learner(s), context, and data collection method.
3. Dataset # Present the learner data clearly.
4. Analytical Focus and Method # State which morphosyntactic feature(s) you selected and explain how you analyzed the data.
5. Findings # Describe the main patterns with supporting examples.
6. Generalizations and Hypotheses # Present your broader conclusions about the learner’s interlanguage knowledge and your hypotheses about why these patterns appear.
7. Connection to SLA Literature # Relate your findings to at least two relevant academic sources.
8. Reflection # Comment briefly on the methodological and theoretical value of working with real learner data.
Part 8. Length Requirement # Suggested length # 1000 words excluding references and appendices Part 9. Submission Format # Naming format for the submission # Name your sumbission as: “Name-QS1”
You may submit as:
a Word document a PDF Part 10. Assessment Criteria # Your work will be evaluated based on the following:
quality and relevance of the learner data clarity of morphosyntactic focus accuracy and depth of analysis strength of pattern-based generalizations quality of theoretical hypotheses ability to connect data to SLA literature organization, clarity, and academic presentation Optional Template for Students # Title # A Mini Analysis of Interlanguage Morphosyntax in Learner A
1. Introduction # State the goal of the analysis and the target feature(s).
2. Learner Background and Data Collection # Introduce the learner and explain how the data was collected.
3. Dataset # Present the learner sentences or utterances.
4. Analytical Focus # Explain which morphosyntactic feature(s) you selected and why.
5. Findings # Describe the main patterns and illustrate them with examples.
6. Generalizations # Summarize the broader regularities in the learner’s language.
7. Hypotheses # Propose theoretically informed explanations.
8. Connection to SLA Literature # Relate your observations to relevant research.
9. Reflection # Explain what this task reveals about learner language and SLA research methods.
Note # This task is not simply an error-hunting exercise. Your goal is to treat learner language as structured evidence of an evolving interlanguage system. A strong submission will move beyond surface correction and will instead show how real learner data can be used to make principled claims about morphosyntactic knowledge, variability, and second language development.

title: Ch.7: Acquisition of Functional Morphology
content:
Chapter 7 — Acquisition of Functional Morphology # Anchor text: Slabakova, R. (2016). Second Language Acquisition. Chapter 7: Acquisition of (Functional) Morphology. Link to Chapter 7
Readings
Representational Deficit Hypothesis: Hawkins and Liszka (2003) Link to Text Hawkins and Casillas (2008) Link to Text Missing Surface Inflectional Hypothesis Prevost and White (2000) Link to Text Prosodic Transfer Hypotheis Goad and White (2004) Link to Text Goad and White (2006) Link to Text Feature Reassembly Hypothesis Lardiere (2007) Link to Text Lardiere (2009) Link to Text Classroom Presentation Instructions # Four readings (highlighted in bold) are to be presented in class.
Each presentation is assigned to one person. Presentations should cover: Research background (language facts, theories, previous findings) Methodology Results Conclusions Time limit: 15 minutes maximum. Interactivity: Presenters are strongly encouraged to design their presentation to be interactive (e.g., brief polls, think‑pair‑share, mini‑tasks for the audience). Slides are required (PowerPoint or PDF). We will begin with students in the linguistics program, but volunteers from any background are very welcome.
1. Pre-Class Preview Guide # 1.1 Chapter Core Focus # This chapter explores how learners acquire functional morphology (grammatical morphemes like -ing, past tense -ed, 3SG -s) in second language (L2) acquisition. It addresses key questions: Do L2 learners follow fixed acquisition orders? Why do they struggle with morphology even if their syntax is intact? And what theories explain these challenges?
1.2 Key Learning Objectives # By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:
Describe the fixed order of L2 functional morphology acquisition and how it relates to L1 patterns. Distinguish between “syntax-before-morphology” and “morphology-before-syntax” views. Compare major hypotheses (RDH, MSIH, PTH, FRH) explaining L2 morphology challenges. Analyze learner data to identify syntax-morphology dissociation and prosodic transfer effects. Explain how universal features are “reassembled” for L2 functional morphology. 1.3 Preview Questions (To Guide Reading) # Why do early L2 studies (e.g., Dulay & Burt) argue for a fixed morpheme order? What evidence supports the “syntax-before-morphology” view (e.g., Patty’s case)? How do RDH and MSIH differ in explaining L2 morphology errors? What is “prosodic transfer,” and how does it affect L2 morphology production? What does the Feature Reassembly Hypothesis (FRH) mean by “reassembling universal features”? Preview & Scaffolding # 1. Why This Preview Matters # Chapter 7 ties 3 areas together:
Morphology: Small word parts (e.g., -ed, -s). Syntax: Sentence structure (e.g., subject-verb order). Meaning: What you want to convey (e.g., past time). This preview clarifies the basics so theories make sense later.
2. Key Morphology Types # Chapter 7 focuses on inflectional morphology (grammar markers)—not derivational (word-creators).
Type What It Does Examples Derivational Makes new words/word classes teach → teacher, happy → unhappiness Inflectional (focus) Adds grammar info (no new word) walk → walks, cat → cats 3. Functional vs. Lexical Morphemes # Functional morphemes = grammar glue (no standalone meaning); lexical = content words (carry ideas).
Type Function Examples What It Adds Lexical Conveys concepts (objects/actions) dog, run, beautiful “What” is happening/being Functional Signals grammar relationships -ed, -s, the, if “When”/“how”/“which one” Example # She walked the dog: Lexical: walked (action), dog (object). Functional: -ed (past time), the (specific dog). 4. Core Functional Morpheme Categories # These are the “grammar tools” Chapter 7 discusses—each links to a syntax “slot” (e.g., Tense Phrase).
Category Example Job Syntax Link Tense/Aspect -ed, -ing Marks when an event happens Tense Phrase (TP) Agreement -s (3SG) Makes subject/verb “match” (e.g., he walks) Agreement Phrase (AgrP) Determiners a, the Marks if a noun is specific Determiner Phrase (DP) Complementizers that, if Links clauses (e.g., I think that she left) Complementizer Phrase (CP) 5. Syntax–Morphology–Meaning: How They Work Together # Grammar is a 3-layer system—learners often master the first two before the third.
Layer What It Does Example Step L2 Common Error 1. Meaning Convey your idea (e.g., past action) “I ate lunch earlier.” None—idea is clear. 2. Syntax Organize words (correct order) I eat lunch earlier Word order is right. 3. Morphology Add grammar markers (surface form) I ate lunch earlier I eat lunch earlier (missing -ed). → Errors usually happen at Layer 3 (morphology)—not meaning/syntax.
6. Functional Categories (Syntax “Slots”) # These are invisible “slots” in sentences that functional morphemes fill (e.g., TP = tense slot).
Category What It Does Example Sentence Link T (Tense) Marks time (past/present) She walks (present) Agr (Agreement) Makes subject/verb match He likes (3SG subject → -s) D (Determiner) Marks specific/non-specific The cat (specific cat) 7. The Big Chapter 7 Question # Chapter 7 debates: Does syntax (structure) come before morphology (form)?
View Core Claim Example Prediction Syntax-before-morphology Structure first, form later He walk = knows TP (needs subject/tense) but misses -s. Morphology-before-syntax Form first, structure later He walk = no TP yet (no tense/agreement slot). Chapter 7 mostly supports syntax-before-morphology (e.g., Patty uses overt subjects but omits -s).
8. Key Term Cheat Sheet # Term Simple Definition Interpretable Feature Adds meaning (e.g., [past] = “before now”) Uninterpretable Feature Grammar-only (e.g., -s = subject-verb match) Mapping Linking abstract grammar to surface form 9. Chapter 7 Roadmap # You’ll learn 4 theories to explain L2 morphology errors:
RDH: Missing grammar “slots” (e.g., no agreement). MSIH: Intact slots, but can’t retrieve the form (e.g., forget -ed). PTH: L1 rhythm affects form (e.g., stressing THE). FRH: Need to “rearrange” grammar features (e.g., L1 vs. L2 tense markers). Use this preview to link each theory to the basics above!
3. Core Content (By Section) # Each section includes Key Takeaways, Core Concepts & Evidence, and Key Study Examples to simplify preview and review.
Section 7.1: Morpheme Studies # Key Takeaways # L2 functional morphology has a (mostly) fixed acquisition order, but early studies overlooked L1 transfer and overuse errors—revised methods (e.g., Stauble’s accuracy) give a more realistic view of “mastery.”
Core Concepts & Evidence # Foundational L1 Precedent: Brown’s (1973) Functor Order
Brown tracked 3 English L1 children and found 14 functional morphemes (e.g., -ing, plural -s) are acquired in a fixed order:
Progressive -ing (19–28 months) → prepositions in/on (27–33 months) → plural -s (27–33 months) → 3SG -s (28–50 months). Order depends on complexity (fewer grammatical features = earlier) and phonetic salience (easier to perceive = earlier). L2 Morpheme Order: Creative Construction Hypothesis
Dulay & Burt (1973, 1974): Spanish/Chinese L1 children learning English showed the same accuracy order (high for -ing/plural -s, low for possessive ’s/3SG -s)—even with different L1s, proving innate grammar (not just L1 transfer) guides acquisition. Bailey et al. (1974): Adults follow the same order as children (e.g., -ing early, 3SG -s late)—fixed order is a general L2 pattern. Criticisms & Method Improvements
Early flaws: Ignored L1 transfer (e.g., Spanish L1 learners master plural -s faster than Japanese L1 learners, as Spanish has plural morphology) and overuse errors (e.g., using -ing for imperatives like Sitting down!). Stauble’s (1984) revised accuracy: Includes overuse in calculations (denominator = obligatory contexts + overused contexts) to avoid overestimating mastery. “Acquired” Cutoff Debates
No universal standard—each reflects a theory:
90% correct (Brown): Measures “full adult-like mastery.” 60% correct: Signals “emerging grammar” (above chance). First productive use: Marks when a structure enters the learner’s grammar. Key Study Example # Dulay & Burt (1973) BSM Task: 5–8-year-old Spanish L1 children with varying English exposure (Sacramento = high, East Harlem = low) all showed congruent accuracy: 85% for -ing, 30% for possessive ’s—proving fixed order. Section 7.2: Syntax-before-morphology # Key Takeaways # L2 learners acquire the syntax of functional categories (e.g., obligatory subjects, tense meaning) first—morphology gaps reflect surface mapping issues, not broken syntax.
Core Concepts & Evidence # Competing Views
Morphology-before-syntax: Learners need surface morphology (e.g., 3SG -s) to “activate” syntax (e.g., TP structure) (Vainikka & Young-Scholten). Syntax-before-morphology (White 2003): Learners master syntactic properties (e.g., overt subjects) first; morphology lags due to mapping challenges (not lack of syntax). Empirical Evidence for Syntax-Morphology Dissociation
Lardiere’s (1998a,b) Patty Case: Mandarin L1 adult L2 English learner with 4.5% accuracy for 3SG -s and 34.5% for past -ed—but 98% overt subjects and 100% nominative case. Her intact syntax proves she has a functional TP; low morphology is a surface issue. Li’s (2012) Child Learners: Mandarin L1 children L2 English show 16% accuracy for 3SG -s but 100% overt subjects—same dissociation as adults. Semantic Support
Slabakova (2003): Bulgarian L1 learners (no L1 tense-aspect morphology) mastered English aspect meanings (e.g., progressive = ongoing) despite poor morphology—proving semantic/syntactic knowledge comes first. Key Study Example # Patty’s TP Performance: She correctly uses overt subjects (He takes the bus, not Takes the bus) and nominative case (he vs. him) but omits 3SG -s (He take). This shows her TP syntax is intact—morphology is the only gap. Section 7.3: Representational Deficit Hypothesis (RDH) # Key Takeaways # RDH argues L2 morphology errors reflect deep syntactic deficits (missing/unvalued features), not just surface issues—but it fails to explain partial accuracy and syntax-morphology dissociation.
Core Concepts & Evidence # RDH Core Claim
Adult L2 learners cannot fully acquire abstract morphosyntactic features absent in their L1. Morphology errors (e.g., missing past -ed) mean the associated syntactic category (e.g., TP) is impaired.
RDH Variants
Variant Core Claim Valueless Features Hypothesis (Eubank) L2 features (e.g., agreement) are “inert” and can’t trigger syntax. Failed Functional Features Hypothesis (Hawkins & Chan) Learners can’t reset L1 parameters (e.g., null subjects). Interpretability Hypothesis (Hawkins et al.) Only meaning-linked features (e.g., noun gender) are acquirable—syntax-only features (e.g., adjective gender concord) are not. Supporting Evidence
Hawkins & Liszka (2003): Chinese L1 learners (no L1 tense morphology) have 63% past -ed accuracy, while German/Japanese L1 learners (with L1 tense) have 92%—RDH attributes this to impaired TP in Chinese learners. Franceschina (2001, 2005): English L1 L2 Spanish learner Martin has 95% accuracy for noun gender (meaning-linked) but 60% for gender concord (syntax-only)—aligns with Interpretability Hypothesis. Limitations
Can’t explain partial accuracy (e.g., 63% past -ed—if TP is impaired, accuracy should be random). Ignores syntax-morphology dissociation (e.g., Patty’s intact TP syntax). Key Study Example # Martin’s Gender Performance: He correctly assigns gender to nouns (el perro = “the dog”) but struggles with adjective concord (el perro negra instead of negro). RDH argues this is because noun gender is meaning-linked (acquirable), while concord is syntax-only (unacquirable). Section 7.4: The Missing Surface Inflection Hypothesis (MSIH) # Key Takeaways # MSIH rejects representational deficits—L2 learners have intact syntax but struggle to map abstract features to surface morphology (e.g., retrieving -s for [3SG] features).
Core Concepts & Evidence # MSIH Core Claim
Morphology is “missing on the surface, not in the syntax.” Learners know syntactic features (e.g., [3SG, present]) but fail to retrieve the corresponding morphology (e.g., -s) during production.
Empirical Evidence
Haznedar & Schwartz (1997) Erdem Case: Turkish L1 L2 English child (4–5 years) uses 90% overt subjects (syntactic finiteness) but 85% uninflected verbs—proves he understands finiteness; morphology retrieval is the issue. Prévost & White (2000a,b) Adult Learners: L2 French/German learners use infinitives in finite positions (e.g., je manger instead of je mange) but avoid finite verbs in non-finite positions—shows they know finiteness rules; they just default to easier-to-retrieve infinitives. Mechanism: Distributed Morphology
Syntax is built first (with features like [3SG]); lexical items (e.g., -s) are inserted late. L2 learners may insert default forms (e.g., infinitive take) if the target (e.g., takes) is inaccessible.
Teaching Relevance
Focus on automatic retrieval: Drill high-frequency inflections (e.g., 3SG -s) in context to reduce retrieval load.
Key Study Example # Erdem’s Development: Early on, he says I play (overt subject = good syntax) but not I playED (missing morphology). Later, his morphology accuracy rises to 60%—proving retrieval improves with practice, not syntax. Section 7.5: The Prosodic Transfer Hypothesis (PTH) # Key Takeaways # PTH adds that L2 morphology gaps come from L1 prosodic transfer—learners apply L1 rules for stress/word structure to L2, misaligning with L2’s prosodic requirements.
Core Concepts & Evidence # Prosodic Structure Basics
Phonology is hierarchical: Segments → Syllables → Feet → Prosodic Words (PWd) → Phonological Phrases. Languages differ in how they attach morphology to these levels (e.g., English -ed is “adjoined” to PWd; Mandarin aspect markers are “integrated” in PWd).
Supporting Evidence
Goad & White (2008) Articles: Mandarin/Turkish L1 L2 English learners stress articles (THE book, A mat)—transferring L1 prosody (Mandarin has no unstressed words; Turkish stresses definite markers). Goad & White (2006) Past Tense: Mandarin L1 learners produce -ed with non-native strong release (e.g., /t/ for played)—transferring Mandarin’s prosodic prominence rules. PTH vs. MSIH
They complement each other: MSIH explains retrieval gaps; PTH explains position/phonetic errors (e.g., omitting articles after disyllabic verbs like catches [the] mat).
Key Study Example # Mandarin L1 Article Stress: Learners say THE cat (stressed the) because Mandarin has no unstressed function words—this is prosodic transfer, not lack of article knowledge (they use the correctly in strong positions). Section 7.6: The Feature Reassembly Hypothesis (FRH) # Key Takeaways # FRH argues L2 morphology acquisition is about reassembling universal features (not learning new ones)—learners adapt L1 feature bundles to L2’s category/form-meaning mappings.
Core Concepts & Evidence # FRH Fundamentals
All languages use universal features (e.g., [past], [gender]). L2 learners:
Identify which features L2 uses. Map features to L2’s lexical category (e.g., [past] on verbs in English, complementizers in Irish). Learn L2’s form-meaning links (e.g., -ed = [past] + [perfective]). Form-Meaning Mismatches: English -ed
Lardiere (2005, 2007) shows -ed encodes 4 meanings (e.g., [+past] = We devoured; politeness = I was wondering). Learners acquire them incrementally (core first, then secondary).
Cross-Linguistic Category Mismatches
Language [past] Feature Host Form L2 Challenge English Verb -ed Mandarin L1: Map [past] to verbs. Irish Complementizer gurL English L1: Map [past] to complementizers. Supporting Evidence: Shimanskaya (2015)
English L1 L2 French learners:
Beginners transfer L1 [Human] (he/she = [+Human], it = [–Human]) to French clitics (le/la = no [Human]), making gender errors for inanimates. Advanced learners drop [Human] and use French’s [gender]-only system (99% accuracy)—proving reassembly. Key Study Example # French Clitic Reassembly: Advanced learners correctly use la for both [+Human] (la fille) and [–Human] (la table)—they reassembled from L1’s [Human]+[gender] to L2’s [gender]-only bundle. 3. Post-Class Review Tools # 3.1 Chapter Takeaways Summary # L2 functional morphology has a fixed order, but L1 transfer and overuse errors modify it. Syntax develops before morphology—low morphology accuracy ≠ broken syntax. RDH (deficits) vs. MSIH (retrieval) vs. PTH (prosody) vs. FRH (reassembly): Together, they explain most L2 morphology gaps. Reassembly of universal features is key for advanced L2 morphology mastery. 3.2 Self-Check Questions # Why did Dulay & Burt’s cross-linguistic study (Spanish/Chinese L1) support the Creative Construction Hypothesis? How does Patty’s case (Lardiere) contradict the Morphology-before-syntax view? What’s the difference between RDH and MSIH in explaining 3SG -s errors? Give an example of prosodic transfer affecting L2 morphology. What does FRH mean by “reassembling” features (use English → Irish [past] as an example)? 3.3 Quick Reference: Hypothesis Comparison # Hypothesis Core Explanation for Morphology Gaps Key Strength Key Weakness RDH Impaired syntactic features (absent in L1) Explains L1 transfer effects Ignores syntax-morphology dissociation MSIH Surface retrieval of morphology Aligns with syntax-before-morphology evidence Doesn’t explain prosodic errors PTH L1 prosodic transfer Explains position/phonetic errors Focuses only on production FRH Reassembling universal features Accounts for cross-linguistic variability Needs more data on beginner reassembly

title: Ch.8: Acquisition of Syntax
content:
Chapter 8 — Acquisition of Syntax # Anchor text: Slabakova, R. (2016). Second Language Acquisition. Chapter 8: Acquisition of Syntax. Link to Chapter 8
Readings
Failed Functional Features Hypothesis Hawkins and Chan (1997) Link to Text Verb Movement White (1990) Link to Text Wh-movement Belikova and White (2009) Link to Text 1. Pre-Class Preview Guide # 1.1 Chapter Core Focus # This chapter explores the acquisition of syntax (sentence structure and grammatical dependencies) in second language (L2) learning, with a focus on three core themes: how the concept of “syntactic parameters” has evolved, whether L2 learners develop native-like syntactic representations, and how cross-linguistic differences (e.g., word order, verb movement, wh-movement) shape acquisition.
1.2 Key Learning Objectives # By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:
Trace the historical evolution of the “parameter” concept—from early “binary switches” to modern feature-based models. Distinguish between Representational Deficit and Full Functional Representation accounts of L2 syntax acquisition. Analyze how L2 learners acquire cross-linguistic word order differences (e.g., SVO vs. SOV) and verb movement patterns (e.g., French vs. English). Explain universal constraints on wh-movement (island constraints) and their role in testing Universal Grammar (UG) access in L2. Interpret empirical data to evaluate which theoretical frameworks best explain L2 syntax acquisition. 1.3 Preview Questions (To Guide Reading) # Why did early “parameter switch” models fail to explain L2 syntax acquisition? What evidence supports the claim that L2 learners can develop native-like syntactic representations (Full Functional Representation)? How do L1 transfer and UG interact in L2 word order acquisition (e.g., Greek SVO → Turkish SOV)? Why do French L1 learners of English struggle with question formation even after mastering adverb placement? What are “island constraints,” and how do they prove UG access in L2 wh-movement acquisition? 2. Core Content Review (By Section) # Each section includes Key Takeaways, Core Concepts & Evidence, and Key Study Examples—aligned with the source document’s modular structure for easy preview/review.
Section 8.1: A Historical Excursion into the Notion of Parameter # Key Takeaways # The concept of “syntactic parameters” (language-specific variation) has evolved from “binary switches” (triggering clusters of constructions) to lexically encoded feature bundles (per the Minimalist Program). Early models failed empirically, while modern frameworks focus on incremental feature reassembly.
Core Concepts & Evidence # Early Parameter Model (1980s–1990s): Binary Switches & Clusters
Core Idea: Parameters are on/off switches paired with universal principles (e.g., Subjacency). A single switch setting triggers a “cluster” of related constructions (like a light switch controlling multiple lights). Flagship Example: Null Subject Parameter (NSP) (Rizzi 1982): Spanish (NSP = On): Allows null subjects (Mangia come una bestia = “He/she eats like a beast”), null expletives (Piove oggi = “It rains today”), and postverbal subjects (Ha telefonato uno studente = “A student called”). English (NSP = Off): Prohibits these constructions (e.g., *Eats like a beast is ungrammatical). Empirical Failures of Early Models
L2 NSP Studies (White 1985, Hilles 1986): Spanish L1 learners of English mastered postverbal subjects but still produced null subjects—contradicting the “cluster” prediction (if one NSP construction is mastered, all should be). Verb Movement Parameter (White 1990): Francophone L2 English learners mastered adverb placement (e.g., John often kisses Mary) but failed at question formation (e.g., *Likes she John?), proving no cluster acquisition. Modern Reconceptualization (2000s–Present): Feature-Based Parameters
Core Idea: Parameters are not switches but universal feature bundles on lexical items (e.g., verbs, complementizers). Languages differ in which features they select and which lexical category hosts them. Example: Tense feature [past] is universal but encoded on: Verbs (English: walked). Complementizers (Irish: gurL thuig sé = “that-Past understood he”). Nouns (Somali: árdday-gii = “student-Det.Masc.Past” = “former student”). Current Thinking: Cognitive Primitives & Sentence Domains
Ramchand & Svenonius (2014) propose a cross-linguistically fixed sentence hierarchy linked to cognition: Verb Domain (V): Encodes the action/state (e.g., Mary eat a sandwich). Tense Domain (T): Anchors the event in time (e.g., Mary ate a sandwich). Complementizer Domain (C): Links the sentence to discourse (e.g., Did Mary eat a sandwich?). Key Study Example # White (1985) NSP Study: Spanish L1 learners of English accepted null subjects 40% of the time (vs. 80% accuracy for French L1 learners) but mastered postverbal subjects—proving NSP does not act as a single switch. Section 8.2: Representational Deficit vs. Full Functional Representation # Key Takeaways # Two frameworks debate L2 syntactic representations: Representational Deficit argues L2 learners have permanent gaps (uninterpretable features absent in L1 cannot be acquired), while Full Functional Representation claims learners develop native-like representations (errors stem from surface performance, not defective syntax).
Core Concepts & Evidence # Representational Deficit Accounts
Core Claim: Adult L2 learners lack access to some universal features—uninterpretable features (regulate syntax, e.g., adjective gender concord) absent in L1 are permanently unacquirable. Key Variants: Fundamental Difference Hypothesis (Bley-Vroman): Learners rely on domain-general strategies (not UG) and L1 transfer—native-like syntax is impossible. Interpretability Hypothesis (Hawkins et al.): Only meaning-linked (interpretable) features (e.g., noun gender) are acquirable; syntax-only features are not. Example (Tsimpli & Dimitrakopoulou 2007): Greek L1 learners of English still accepted ungrammatical resumptive pronouns (*Who do you think that Susan would marry him?) at advanced stages—claimed as proof of permanent deficit. Full Functional Representation Accounts
Core Claim: L2 learners have intact syntactic representations—errors come from surface issues (e.g., feature mapping, lexical retrieval), not defective syntax. Key Variants: Full Transfer Full Access (FTFA, Schwartz & Sprouse): Learners transfer L1 features initially but retain UG access to reset parameters. Missing Surface Inflection Hypothesis (MSIH, Prévost & White): Syntax is intact; morphology gaps reflect mapping challenges (e.g., Patty’s 4.5% 3SG -s accuracy but 98% overt subject accuracy, Lardiere 1998a,b). Example (Leal Méndez & Slabakova 2014): Advanced French L1 learners of English rejected ungrammatical [Human] pronoun errors (*It is Mary) at 92% accuracy—matching natives (96%), proving no permanent deficit. Empirical Test Cases
Test Case Representational Deficit Prediction Full Functional Prediction Outcome (Supports) English [Human] pronoun feature (French L1) Cannot acquire [Human]—accept *It is Mary Acquire [Human]—reject *It is Mary Full Functional Wh-island constraints (Chinese L1) Cannot acquire Subjacency—accept *Who did you wonder whether… Acquire Subjacency—reject ungrammatical sentences Full Functional Key Study Example # Patty’s Case (Lardiere 1998a,b): Mandarin L1 L2 English learner with 4.5% 3SG -s accuracy but 98% overt subject accuracy—proves TP (Tense Phrase) syntax is intact; only surface morphology is missing (supports MSIH). Section 8.3: Word Order # Key Takeaways # L2 word order acquisition starts with L1 transfer but progresses to L2 norms via UG. Canonical orders (e.g., Turkish SOV) are acquired early, while non-canonical orders (e.g., Turkish OSV) require integrating multiple features (word order + case + specificity)—slowing progress.
Core Concepts & Evidence # Cross-Linguistic Word Order: Prevalence & Cognitive Roots
Typological Dominance: SVO (~35.4%, e.g., English) and SOV (~45%, e.g., Turkish) dominate because they align with human cognition (Agent → Action → Patient). Rare Orders: VSO (e.g., Irish) and OSV are rare—L2 acquisition is slower due to cognitive dissonance. Theoretical Evolution of Word Order
1980s: VP Headedness Parameter: SVO = head-initial VP (verb before object); SOV = head-final VP (verb after object). 1990s (Kayne 1994): Universal SVO: All languages have underlying SVO—SOV results from object movement to pre-verbal position. 2000s+: Lexical Diacritics: Verbs carry diacritics (e.g., English eat = [+pre-object]; Turkish yemek = [+post-object])—L2 learners acquire these to produce correct order. L2 Word Order Acquisition: Transfer & UG
Early Transfer (FTFA): Greek L1 (SVO) learners of Turkish (SOV) initially produce SVO (Mary yedi bir elma = “Mary ate an apple”) but shift to SOV (Mary bir elma yedi) with input (Papadopoulou et al. 2011). Feature Interaction Challenge: Non-canonical orders (e.g., Turkish OSV: Bir elma Mary yedi = “An apple Mary ate”) require integrating word order, Accusative case (-i), and specificity—intermediate learners have 49% case accuracy (vs. 95% verbal inflection), limiting OSV mastery. Key Study Example # Papadopoulou et al. (2011) Greek-Turkish Study: Beginners mastered Turkish SOV (canonical order) but failed at OSV (non-canonical, needs case + specificity). Advanced learners improved OSV accuracy to 72%—proving incremental feature integration. Section 8.4: Verb Movement # Key Takeaways # Verb movement (verbs moving to Tense/Complementizer vs. staying in Verb Phrase) is not a parametric switch—L2 acquisition involves incremental feature mapping. The Verb-Second (V2) rule (German) is acquired late due to rare input but mastered by advanced learners.
Core Concepts & Evidence # Cross-Linguistic Verb Movement: French vs. English
French: Verbs move to Tense (T)/Complementizer (C)—supports verb-adverb (S-V-Adv-O: Jean embrasse souvent Marie), verb-negation (S-V-Neg-O: Marie n’aime pas Jean), and question inversion (V-S-O: Aime-t-elle Jean?). English: Verbs stay in Verb Phrase (VP)—requires adverb before verb (S-Adv-V-O: John often kisses Mary), do-support for negation/questions (S-Aux-Neg-V-O: Mary does not like John). Early Verb Movement Parameter: Failed Cluster Predictions
White (1990) Francophone L2 English Study: Learners taught adverb placement showed no improvement in question formation—proving no cluster acquisition (undermines “switch” model). Verb-Second (V2) Rule: German Case Study
V2 Rule: Finite verbs must be the second constituent in German main clauses (e.g., Im Park hat er sie gefunden = “In the park had he her found”).
