L2 Acquisition: Beginners: 49.3% V2 violations (e.g., *Im Park er hat sie gefunden = “In the park he had her found”). Advanced: 100% accuracy (Conradie 2006)—explained by Yang’s Variational Learning Model (rare unambiguous V2 input: 1.2% of child-directed speech) and Multiple Grammars Hypothesis (coexisting L1/L2 subgrammars). Key Study Example # Conradie (2006) Afrikaans V2 Study: South African English L1 learners of Afrikaans (V2 language) showed 100% V2 accuracy at advanced stages—proving UG access to complex verb movement. Section 8.5: Wh-movement # Key Takeaways # Wh-movement (wh-phrases moving to clause start) is constrained by universal “island rules” (prohibiting movement out of certain structures). L2 learners acquire these constraints via UG—proving Full Functional Representation, even if L1 lacks wh-movement.
Core Concepts & Evidence # Cross-Linguistic Wh-movement: In-situ vs. Movement
Wh-movement Languages (English): Wh-phrases move to CP (e.g., What did John buy?; *John bought what? is ungrammatical for regular questions). Wh-in-situ Languages (Mandarin): Wh-phrases stay in base position (e.g., Hufei mai-le shenme? = “Hufei bought what?”). Island Constraints: Universal Limits
Island types (prohibit wh-movement out of bounded structures): Wh-islands: *Who did you wonder whether this girl danced with? Complex NP islands: *Who did you spread a rumor that this girl danced with? Poverty of the Stimulus: Learners never hear ungrammatical island sentences—acquiring constraints proves UG access. L2 Wh-movement: Evidence for UG
Martohardjono (1993): Chinese/Indonesian L1 learners of English rejected strong island violations (87%/76% accuracy) more than weak ones—mirroring natives (99%/78% accuracy), proving UG access. Li (1998): Chinese L1 learners in China (classroom input) and Canada (naturalistic input) had comparable island constraint accuracy—input type does not block UG use. Key Study Example # Johnson & Newport (1991) Chinese L1 Study: Adult Chinese L1 learners of English reliably distinguished grammatical (non-island) and ungrammatical (island) wh-movement—accuracy above chance, proving Subjacency acquisition via UG. 3. Post-Class Review Tools # 3.1 Chapter Takeaways Summary # Parameters evolved from “switches” to feature bundles—L2 acquisition involves incremental feature reassembly, not holistic switch-setting. Full Functional Representation better explains L2 syntax: Learners develop native-like representations; errors are surface issues (not deficits). Word order/verb movement acquisition starts with L1 transfer but progresses via UG—complexity rises with feature interaction. Wh-movement island constraints are acquired via UG—proof of innate syntactic principles in L2. 3.2 Self-Check Questions # Why did early parameter models (e.g., NSP cluster) fail to explain L2 syntax acquisition? How does Patty’s case (Lardiere 1998a,b) support Full Functional Representation? What makes Turkish OSV (non-canonical word order) harder to acquire than SOV (canonical)? Why is German V2 acquired late by L2 learners (per Yang’s model)? How do island constraints prove UG access in L2 wh-movement acquisition? 3.3 Quick Reference: Framework Comparison # Framework Core Claim About L2 Syntax Key Strength Key Weakness Representational Deficit Permanent gaps (uninterpretable features unacquirable) Explains L1 transfer effects Ignores native-like advanced performance Full Functional Representation Native-like representations (errors = surface issues) Aligns with UG access evidence Needs more data on beginner feature reassembly

title: Ch.10: Acquisition of the Syntax-Semantics Interface
content:
Chapter 10 — Acquisition of the Syntax-Semantics Interface # Anchor text: Slabakova, R. (2016). Second Language Acquisition. Chapter 10: Acquisition of the Syntax–Semantics Interface. Link to Chapter 10
⭐ Overview # The five key types of meaning in language: lexical, phrasal (sentential) semantic, grammatical, discourse-related, and pragmatic—and how they interact with syntax . Syntax–semantics mismatches: When universal meanings (e.g., ongoing/habitual events) are encoded by different forms across languages (e.g., English past progressive vs. Spanish Imperfect) . Poverty of the Stimulus (POS) in semantics: How L2 learners acquire meanings not attested in input (e.g., missing interpretations of impersonal se in Spanish preterit) . Special learning challenges: novel constructions (e.g., French discontinuous interrogatives) and morphologically unmarked meanings (e.g., English articles for Russian/Korean learners) . 🎯 Learning goals # By the end of Week 10 you should be able to:
Distinguish the five types of meaning (lexical to pragmatic) and explain how syntax shapes their computation (e.g., word order affecting topic meaning) . Identify a syntax–semantics mismatch using examples (e.g., English vs. Spanish aspectual tenses) and predict L2 acquisition challenges . Explain why semantic POS situations (e.g., quantifier scope in Japanese) require UG access—since negative evidence is absent . Apply the Article Choice Parameter to explain why Russian/Korean learners of English fluctuate between definiteness and specificity when using articles . 📖 Reading (do before class) # Required: Slabakova (2016), Chapter 10 (focus on Sections 10.1–10.6; prioritize mismatches and POS over technical exercises). As you read, note: How L1 transfer affects syntax–semantics mappings (e.g., Bulgarian learners of English acquiring bare verb perfectivity) . Why pragmatic meaning (e.g., scalar implicatures) is computed after semantic meaning (“semantics proposes, pragmatics disposes”) . Guiding questions while you read
Why do English The tigers eat meat and Spanish Los tigres comen carne have different meanings (specific only vs. generic/specific)? How do advanced L2 learners acquire the missing interpretation of Spanish impersonal se (no generic reading in preterit) without negative input? Why do Russian learners of English sometimes use the with indefinite specific NPs (e.g., “I want to sell the beautiful necklace”)? 🧠 Key terms # syntax–semantics interface; lexical meaning; phrasal semantics; grammatical meaning; discourse-related meaning; pragmatic meaning; scalar implicatures; syntax–semantics mismatch; Poverty of the Stimulus (POS); Article Choice Parameter; definiteness; specificity; discontinuous interrogatives; impersonal se
10.1 Types of Meaning # Meaning in language has 5 interconnected layers—all work together to convey a complete message.
Core Types & Examples # Meaning Type Definition Key Example (from Chapter) L2 Learning Tip Lexical Literal, primary meaning of individual words (stored in mental lexicon). English cat = Italian gatto (both = “small furry animal”); tea = drink/dried leaves/evening meal (UK). Map L2 words to existing concepts (e.g., gatto → “cat”) or learn new lexical meanings (e.g., tea = “evening meal”). Phrasal (Sentential) Semantic Compositional (calculated by combining words + rules) — can have multiple interpretations. English: Cats were exterminated = “some cats” or “all cats”; Italian: Gatti sono stati sterminati = only “some cats.” Watch for cross-linguistic differences in how plural nouns/word order shape meaning. Grammatical Encoded in inflectional morphology (tense, agreement) — adds structural info. Jane eats (present habitual) vs. Jane ate (past completed/habitual); -ed = past, -s = 3SG agreement. Master grammatical morphemes to avoid meaning gaps (e.g., omitting -ed = unclear time). Discourse-Related Depends on prior context (links sentence to conversation). Question: Does Jane like sushi? Answer: Sushi, she eats; sashimi, she adores (fronting = topic focus). Pay attention to how context shapes word order (e.g., fronted objects = topic). Pragmatic Inferential (implied, not direct) — relies on context/Gricean maxims. Bonnie ate some strawberries = “some but not all” (pragmatic) vs. “some possibly all” (logical); Today is Tuesday (denotation changes daily). Learn to infer implied meaning (e.g., “some” ≠ “all” in English). Integration Example: Mona likes tea # Lexical: Mona = name, likes = “feels positive toward,” tea = “drink.” Phrasal Semantic: Mona (Experiencer) → likes → tea (Theme) = “Mona favors tea.” Grammatical: -s = 3SG agreement, present tense = habitual. Discourse-Related: Neutral word order = new statement (not a response). Pragmatic: Inferred = “Mona likes to drink tea” (not “watch tea”). 10.2 Mismatches at the Syntax–Semantics Interface # Key Idea: All languages convey the same universal meanings (e.g., “habitual past”), but use different forms to encode them — this “mismatch” causes L2 errors.
What Is a Mismatch? # No missing meanings — just different form-meaning links (e.g., English uses simple past for habitual past; Spanish uses Imperfect). L2 Challenge: Unlearn L1 mappings and adopt L2-specific ones (not just memorize words). Two Core Mismatches (with Examples) # 1. Aspectual Tenses (English vs. Spanish) # Universal semantic primitives: One-time completed event, habitual event, ongoing event.
Language Form Mapped Meanings Example English Simple Past One-time completed + habitual Felix robbed people (habitual) / Felix robbed a person (one-time) English Past Progressive Only ongoing Felix was robbing when police arrived Spanish Preterit (-ó) Only one-time completed Guillermo robó = “Guillermo robbed someone once” Spanish Imperfect (-aba) Habitual + ongoing Guillermo robaba = “Guillermo robbed habitually” / “was robbing” L2 Error: Spanish L1 learners say *Felix was robbing people (to mean habitual) — transfers Spanish Imperfect’s “habitual” mapping to English past progressive (only ongoing). 2. Politeness Marking (English vs. German/Bulgarian/Russian) # Language Polite Form (Singular Addressee) Informal Form English Equivalent German Sie (2PL pronoun) du (2SG) “Sir/Madam” (lexical) Bulgarian Vie (2PL) ti (2SG) “Excuse me, Sir” Russian vy (2PL) ty (2SG) “Miss” English No morphological marker you (all uses) “Excuse me, do you know the time?” L2 Error: German L1 learners say *Do Sie know the time? — transfers German’s plural pronoun for politeness to English (uses lexical terms instead). 10.3 L2 Acquisition of Syntax–Semantics Mismatches # Key Idea: Mismatches are acquirable! Learners transfer L1 mappings initially but adopt target L2 links with proficiency.
Study 1: Slabakova (2003) — Bulgarian L1 → English Aspect # Mismatch: English bare verbs (e.g., I saw Mary cross) entail completion ([+perfective] feature); Bulgarian equivalents do not. Participants: 112 Bulgarian L2 English learners (low → advanced) + native controls. Tasks: Production (check inflection knowledge) + Truth Value Judgment Task (TVJT) — judge if sentences match stories. Story Context English Test Sentence Expected Judgment Why? Matt ate half a cake (incomplete) I observed Matt eat a cake False Bare verb = completion required. Matt ate half a cake (incomplete) I observed Matt eating a cake True -ing = no completion required. Alicia ate a whole cake (complete) I watched Alicia eat a cake True Bare verb = completion matches. Results: Advanced learners: 95% accuracy on untaught [+perfective] feature (even more than natives). Intermediate learners: Improved with proficiency (68% → 83% → 95%). Takeaway: Syntax comes before semantics — learners first master English’s “impoverished” verb morphology, then the linked [+perfective] meaning. Study 2: Ionin et al. — Genericity (English vs. Spanish/Portuguese) # Mismatch: English uses bare plurals for generic meaning (Tigers eat meat) and definite plurals for specific (The tigers eat meat); Spanish uses definite plurals for both (Los tigres comen carne = generic + specific). Results: Initial L1 transfer: Spanish L1 learners overuse the for generic (*The tigers eat meat); English L1 learners use bare plurals in Spanish (*Tigres comen carne). Advanced learners: Retreat to target — Spanish L1 uses English bare plurals; English L1 uses Spanish definite plurals. Takeaway: Identifying ungrammatical forms (e.g., Spanish bare plurals) is easier than mastering all interpretations. 10.4 Poverty of the Stimulus (POS) in Semantics # Key Idea: Learners acquire “unavailable meanings” (e.g., a sentence can’t mean X) without explicit teaching — Universal Grammar (UG) guides them.
What Is POS? # Two similar sentences: One has two meanings, the other has one (missing meaning = unavailable). Input never shows “this sentence can’t mean X” — learners use UG to infer constraints. Study 1: Spanish Impersonal se # POS Property: se + Imperfect = two meanings (generic: “people in general” + specific: “we”); se + Preterit = only specific (“we”). Example: Se comía bien en casa de la abuela = “People ate well” / “We ate well.” Se comió bien en casa de la abuela = only “We ate well” (generic = unavailable). Results: Advanced L2 Spanish learners (L1 English) = 85% accurate in rejecting generic for Preterit — UG guides interpretation. Study 2: Japanese Distributive Quantifiers # POS Property: Canonical SOV order (Dareka-ga dono hon-mo yonda) = only S > O scope (“one person read all books”); scrambled OSV order = two scopes (S > O + O > S).
Results:
Korean L1 learners (L1 = same as Japanese) = 95% accurate (transfer). English L1 learners (L1 = allows O > S in canonical order) = half mastered the POS constraint (rejected O > S for SOV) — UG overcomes transfer. Takeaway: POS knowledge is acquirable via UG, even in adult L2 learning.
10.5 Meaning of Novel Constructions # Key Idea: Novel constructions (no L1 equivalent) require learning syntax first — semantic constraints follow via universal mechanisms.
What Is a Novel Construction? # L2 structure with no direct L1 equivalent (e.g., French discontinuous interrogatives — English can’t split wh-phrases). French Continuous vs. Discontinuous Interrogatives # Construction Type Example Allowable Interpretations of de célèbre (“famous”) Continuous Qui de célèbre fumait dans les années 70? Past (Al Green) + present (Oprah Winfrey) celebrities Discontinuous Qui fumait de célèbre dans les années 70? Only past celebrities (Al Green) Why? Syntax determines meaning: Continuous: de célèbre = above past tense → past/present fame. Discontinuous: de célèbre = below past tense → only past fame. Study: Dekydtspotter & Sprouse (2001) # Participants: English L1 learners of French (intermediate → advanced). Task: Judge if answers (Al Green/Oprah) fit questions (continuous/discontinuous). Results: Advanced learners: 90% accuracy (rejected Oprah for discontinuous questions) — matched natives. Takeaway: Once learners master the construction’s syntax, universal semantic rules (not input) guide meaning. 10.6 Conjuring Up Something from Nothing # Key Idea: Learners acquire dedicated morphological markers (e.g., English articles the/a) for semantic features their L1 encodes via non-morphological means (context, word order).
Core Features: Definiteness vs. Specificity # Feature Definition Example Definiteness Shared knowledge (speaker + hearer know the referent) The car was red (car mentioned earlier). Specificity Speaker knows the referent (hearer doesn’t) Jill wants to marry a Canadian (she has someone specific in mind). Article Choice Parameter (Ionin et al., 2004) # Languages with two articles use one of two settings: Definiteness (English): the = definite, a = indefinite. Specificity (Samoan): le = specific, se = nonspecific. L2 Prediction: Learners from article-less L1s (Russian/Korean) fluctuate between settings before settling on target. Study Results: Russian/Korean L1 → English Articles # Fluctuation:
Definite NPs: 79% the for specific definites vs. 57% for nonspecific (overused a). Indefinite NPs: 84% a for nonspecific vs. 54% for specific (overused the). Proficiency Effect: Advanced learners showed less fluctuation.
L2 Challenges:
Feature overlap (definiteness ≈ specificity) → confusion. No L1 morphology to transfer → test universal settings. Context dependence → track speaker-hearer shared knowledge. Chapter 10 Key Takeaways for L2 Learners # Meaning is multilayered — focus on form-meaning links, not just words. Mismatches and POS properties are acquirable via UG and proficiency. Initial L1 transfer is normal — target mappings emerge with exposure. Syntax often precedes semantics — master structure first, then meaning constraints. Pragmatic and discourse meaning require context practice (not just rules). Use these notes to connect theory to your own L2 learning — notice how you navigate form-meaning mappings in your target language!

title: Ch.11: Acquisition of the Syntax-Discourse & Semantics-Pragmatics Interfaces
content:
Chapter 11 — Acquisition of the Syntax-Discourse & Semantics-Pragmatics Interfaces # Anchor text: Slabakova, R. (2016). Second Language Acquisition. Chapter 11: Acquisition of the Syntax–Discourse and Semantics–Pragmatics Interfaces. Link to Chapter 11
⭐ Overview # The two key external interfaces: Syntax–Discourse Interface: How syntax encodes discourse information (e.g., Topic/Focus via word order, clitics) . Semantics–Pragmatics Interface: How context and universal pragmatic principles (e.g., Gricean maxims) adjust literal meaning (e.g., scalar implicatures) . Why interface properties are often harder to acquire: They require integrating linguistic (syntax/semantics) and extralinguistic (context/culture) information—taxing working memory . Key phenomena: Topic/Focus marking (clitic doubling, word order), pronoun reference (null/overt pronoun division of labor), intonation as discourse cue, and scalar implicatures . 🎯 Learning goals # By the end of Week 11 you should be able to:
Distinguish the syntax–discourse interface (e.g., clitic doubling for Topic) from the semantics–pragmatics interface (e.g., scalar implicatures) and explain why both rely on context . Describe how languages mark Topic/Focus (e.g., English topicalization vs. Spanish clitic left dislocation) and predict L2 acquisition challenges . Apply the Interface Hypothesis to explain why near-native learners struggle with pronoun reference (e.g., Italian overt pronouns for Topic shift) . Explain why scalar implicatures (e.g., some = “not all”) are universal but may still be processed differently in L2—especially under cognitive load . 📖 Reading (do before class) # Required: Slabakova (2016), Chapter 11 (focus on Sections 11.1–11.6; prioritize interface definitions and key phenomena over technical exercises). As you read, note: How L1 transfer affects interface acquisition (e.g., Turkish learners of Dutch transferring null pronoun reference rules) . Why frequency of interface constructions (e.g., English topicalization is rare) impacts learning success . Guiding questions while you read
Why do Spanish learners of English struggle with topicalization (The wine she didn’t drink vs. The wine she didn’t drink it)? How do Italian native speakers use null vs. overt pronouns to signal Topic maintenance vs. Topic shift? Why do adult L2 learners compute scalar implicatures more accurately than L1 children but less consistently than L1 adults? 🧠 Key terms # syntax–discourse interface; semantics–pragmatics interface; Topic; Focus (presentational/contrastive); clitic doubling; topicalization; Interface Hypothesis; pronoun reference (division of labor); intonation (nuclear stress); scalar implicatures; Gricean maxims (Quantity Maxim); deaccenting
CHAPTER 11: ACQUISITION OF THE SYNTAX–DISCOURSE & SEMANTICS–PRAGMATICS INTERFACES # Core Goal: Understand how L2 learners integrate syntax/semantics with discourse context and pragmatic principles—and why these interfaces are uniquely challenging.
11.1 Defining the Interfaces # External interfaces connect core grammar to context—unlike internal interfaces (e.g., syntax–semantics) which are language-internal:
Interface Core Function Key Phenomena Syntax–Discourse Encodes discourse status (Topic = old info; Focus = new info) via syntax Clitic doubling, topicalization, VS word order, pronoun reference Semantics–Pragmatics Adjusts literal (semantic) meaning via context/world knowledge Scalar implicatures, deixis (this/that), anaphoric deaccenting Key Distinction: Syntax–discourse relies on prior discourse (e.g., “The wine” = Topic because it was mentioned earlier); semantics–pragmatics relies on universal principles (e.g., Grice’s Quantity Maxim) . 11.2 Marking Topic & Focus Across Languages # Languages use different syntactic strategies to signal Topic (old info) and Focus (new info)—mismatches between L1 and L2 create acquisition challenges:
1. Clitic Doubling for Topic # Spanish/Bulgarian: Topicalized objects require a clitic pronoun (doubling) to signal old info. Example: Spanish: A Pedro, no lo saludó (“Pedro, I didn’t greet him”) → lo = clitic doubling Topic Pedro . Bulgarian: *Vinoto tja ne (go) pi (“The wine she didn’t drink it”) → go = mandatory clitic for Topic vinoto . English: Topicalized objects forbid resumptive pronouns: *The wine she didn’t drink (it) . Acquisition Findings: Advanced English learners of Bulgarian master clitic doubling for Topic (Ivanov 2009) . Spanish learners of English struggle to omit resumptive pronouns in topicalization (Slabakova & García Mayo 2015)—due to English topicalization’s rarity in input . 2. Word Order for Focus # Spanish (null-subject language): VS word order signals presentational Focus (new info): Q: ¿Quién gritó? (“Who shouted?”) → A: Gritó una mujer (“Shouted a woman”) . Neutral context (out of blue): VS preferred for unaccusative verbs (Vino la policía = “Arrived the police”) but not unergative verbs (Una mujer gritó = “A woman shouted”) . English: Fixed SV order; Focus marked via intonation (e.g., A WOMAN shouted) . Acquisition Findings: English learners of Spanish master SV/VS distinction for unaccusative/unergative verbs but fail to link VS to Focus (Lozano 2006)—supports the Interface Hypothesis (discourse integration is taxing) . 11.3 Pronoun Reference at the Syntax–Discourse Interface # Null and overt pronouns have a “division of labor” in discourse—this is a classic interface property:
1. Romance Languages (Spanish/Italian) # Null Pronouns: Signal Topic maintenance (embedded subject = main clause subject). Example: Italian: La vecchietta saluta la ragazza quando attraversa la strada (“The old lady greets the girl when [she] crosses the street”) → attraversa = null pronoun = old Topic (la vecchietta) . Overt Pronouns: Signal Topic shift (embedded subject = new referent). Example: Italian: La vecchietta saluta la ragazza quando lei attraversa la strada (“The old lady greets the girl when she crosses the street”) → lei = overt pronoun = new referent (la ragazza) . 2. L2 Acquisition Challenges # Near-Native Learners: Less sensitive to Topic shift—30% of Italian near-natives interpret overt pronouns as Topic maintenance (vs. 5% of natives) (Belletti et al. 2007) . Heritage Speakers: May never acquire the division of labor (Shin & Cairns 2009)—exposed to English before age 7 (when Topic shift sensitivity emerges in L1) . Chinese Learners of English: Master null object reference (e.g., Xiao Zhang says Lao Wang likes ø) by advanced proficiency—showing interface success is possible with clear input . 11.4 Intonation as a Discourse Cue # Intonation (nuclear stress, deaccenting) signals Focus/Topic—but L1 prosodic rules transfer and complicate L2 learning:
1. English vs. Spanish Prosody # English: Nuclear Stress (NS) is flexible—marks Focus on any constituent. Example: Q: Who broke his leg? → A: A BOY broke his leg (NS on Focus boy) . Anaphoric Deaccenting: Old info loses stress (e.g., Q: Why buy that stamp? → A: Because I COLLECT stamps—NS shifts to collect because stamps is old info) . Spanish: NS is fixed (last constituent) — Focus marked via word order (not intonation) . 2. Acquisition Findings # Spanish learners of English acquire deaccenting (new rule) before restructuring NS (L1 transfer) (Nava & Zubizarreta 2009) . Advanced learners still struggle with NS flexibility—prefer L1-like fixed stress (Zubizarreta & Nava 2011) . 11.5 Scalar Implicatures at the Semantics–Pragmatics Interface # Scalar implicatures (e.g., some = “not all”) are universal but require cognitive effort—explaining L2 processing differences:
1. How Implicatures Work # Logical Meaning: Some professors are smart = “some and possibly all” . Pragmatic Meaning: Some professors are smart = “not all professors are smart” (via Grice’s Quantity Maxim: “Be as informative as required”) . 2. L2 Acquisition Findings # Universal Mechanisms: Korean learners of English compute implicatures at 60% (vs. natives’ 40%) in L2—better than L1 children (Slabakova 2010) . Processing Load: Learners struggle with indirect implicatures (e.g., Max didn’t read all the books = “Max read some”)—more cognitively demanding than direct implicatures (Lieberman 2009) . Bilingual Advantage: Bilingual children outperform monolinguals on Gricean maxims (relevance, politeness) but not on scalar implicatures—suggests different processing demands (Siegal et al. 2009) . 11.6 The Interface Hypothesis & Key Conclusions # Interface Hypothesis (Sorace 2011): External interfaces (syntax–discourse, semantics–pragmatics) are more vulnerable than internal interfaces—due to working memory strain from integrating linguistic/contextual info . Nuance: Interface difficulty is not universal—frequency of constructions matters: Spanish clitic left dislocation (common) is acquired easily; English topicalization (rare) is not (Slabakova 2015) . Final Takeaways: Syntax–discourse properties require matching L2 syntax to discourse context—challenged by L1 transfer and input rarity . Semantics–pragmatics properties (implicatures) are universal but taxed by L2 processing load . Near-native learners may show residual optionality at interfaces—but success is possible with sufficient input . Preview/Review Questions # Preview # What is the difference between “Topic maintenance” and “Topic shift”? How do pronouns signal this? Why is anaphoric deaccenting (English) harder for Spanish learners than deaccenting (Spanish)? Review # How does the Interface Hypothesis explain why near-native Italian learners misinterpret overt pronouns? Why do English learners of Spanish master VS word order for unaccusative verbs but not for Focus? What evidence shows scalar implicatures are universal but cognitively demanding in L2? –>

title: Term Research Proposal Guidelines: Generative Second Language Acquisition (SLA)
content:
Term Research Proposal Guidelines # Generative Second Language Acquisition (SLA) # 1. Overview # This assignment requires you to design a small-scale original research proposal grounded in generative approaches to SLA. Your proposal should identify a clear theoretical problem in generative SLA, formulate well-defined research questions, and outline a methodologically appropriate study informed by existing generative literature. The goal is to demonstrate your ability to connect generative theory with empirical research design.
2. Core Principles of Generative SLA # Your proposal must be explicitly grounded in generative linguistics. Appropriate topics include:
Accessibility of Universal Grammar (UG) in adult L2 acquisition Acquisition of syntactic and semantic features, parameters, and functional categories Interface issues in L2 acquisition (e.g., syntax–semantics, syntax–pragmatics) Feature reassembly and form–meaning mappings Representational vs. processing-based explanations of L2 behavior Cross-linguistic influence (CLI) under UG constraints Avoid purely pedagogical, sociocultural, or behavioral approaches unless they directly engage with generative theory.
3. Required Structure # 3.1 Topic # Provide a 1–2 sentence statement clearly identifying:
the L2 phenomenon the generative construct(s) involved (e.g., UG access, parameter setting, feature reassembly). The topic must be theoretically motivated, not instructional in nature.
3.2 Introduction # Theoretical Problem
Describe the generative SLA issue your study addresses (e.g., UG accessibility, feature deficits, parameter resetting). Explain why this problem matters for generative theory. Study Purpose
State how your study addresses this problem.
Specify:
the target feature(s) or structure(s) the L1–L2 pairing why this pairing is theoretically informative. 3.3 Literature Review # Review key generative theories relevant to your topic (e.g., FRH, RDH, MSIH).
Summarize empirical findings from generative SLA studies.
Identify:
theoretical gaps (unresolved debates) methodological gaps (e.g., overreliance on offline tasks) cross-linguistic gaps. Clearly state how your study addresses these gaps.
3.4 Research Question(s) # Pose one primary research question that directly tests a generative hypothesis. Optional: include 1–2 secondary questions. Questions must target linguistic representations, not surface accuracy or pedagogy. Explicitly connect the question(s) to the identified gap(s). 3.5 Methodology # Your methods must be generatively motivated.
Method
Specify the overall design (e.g., experimental, mixed-methods). Justify task choice with reference to generative SLA research. Participants
Define L1–L2 pairing, proficiency levels, and sample size. Justify all choices theoretically. Tasks & Data
Describe tasks (e.g., GJT, self-paced reading, elicited production). Explain how each task tests the target generative construct. Analysis
Specify:
dependent and independent variables statistical or coding procedures Explain how different outcomes would support competing generative accounts.
3.6 Expected Results and Discussion (Optional) # Briefly outline expected patterns based on generative theory. Discuss how alternative outcomes would be interpreted theoretically. Note key limitations. 3.7 Conclusion (Optional) # Restate the central theoretical question. Summarize the study’s contribution to generative SLA. Suggest directions for future research. 3.8 References # Minimum 15 scholarly sources in generative SLA. Use a consistent academic citation style. 4. Evaluation Criteria # Proposals will be assessed on:
Clarity of generative theoretical alignment Depth and accuracy of literature engagement Quality and relevance of the research question(s) Methodological appropriateness for testing generative hypotheses Overall coherence and scholarly writing quality 5. Formatting Requirements # Language: The proposal may be written in English or Chinese. Length: Suggested length 3,000–4,000 words (excluding references). Submissions slightly shorter or longer are acceptable if the theoretical argument and research design are clearly and adequately developed. Font & Spacing: 12-point Times New Roman (or 宋体 for Chinese text), 1.5-line spacing. File Format: PDF or Word document.
